{{Short description|Spatial geometry with curvature}}
{{Spacetime|cTopic=Relation to gravity}}

'''Curved space''' often refers to a [[spatial geometry]] which is not "flat", where a ''[[flat space]]'' has zero [[curvature]], as described by [[Euclidean geometry]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Feynman Lectures on Physics Vol. II Ch. 42: Curved Space |url=https://www.feynmanlectures.caltech.edu/II_42.html#:~:text=In%20general,%20a%20two-dimensional,of%20discrepancy%20or%20the%20other. |access-date=2024-01-18 |website=www.feynmanlectures.caltech.edu}}</ref> Curved spaces can generally be described by [[Riemannian geometry]], though some simple cases can be described in other ways. 

Curved spaces play an essential role in [[general relativity]], where [[gravity]] is often visualized as ''[[curved spacetime]]''.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Curved Space |url=https://www.math.brown.edu/tbanchof/STG/ma8/papers/dstanke/Project/curved_space.html |access-date=2024-01-18 |website=www.math.brown.edu}}</ref> The [[Friedmann–Lemaître–Robertson–Walker metric]] is a curved metric which forms the current foundation for the description of the [[expansion of the universe]] and the [[shape of the universe]].{{Citation needed|date=January 2024}}  The fact that photons have no mass yet are distorted by gravity, means that the explanation would have to be something besides photonic mass.  Hence, the belief that large bodies curve space and so light, traveling on the curved space will, appear as being subject to gravity.  It is not, but it is subject to the curvature of space.

==Simple two-dimensional example==
A very familiar example of a curved space is the surface of a sphere. While to our familiar outlook the sphere ''looks'' three-dimensional, if an object is constrained to lie on the surface, it only has [[Two-dimensional space|two dimensions]] that it can move in. The surface of a sphere can be completely described by two dimensions, since no matter how rough the surface may appear to be, it is still only a surface, which is the two-dimensional outside border of a volume. Even the surface of the Earth, which is fractal in complexity, is still only a two-dimensional boundary along the outside of a volume.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Curved Space - Special and General Relativity - The Physics of the Universe |url=https://www.physicsoftheuniverse.com/topics_relativity_curved.html |access-date=2024-01-18 |website=www.physicsoftheuniverse.com}}</ref>

==Embedding==
[[Image:Pythagorean triangle.png|thumb|In a flat space, the sum of the squares of the side of a right-angled triangle is equal to the square of the hypotenuse. This relationship does not hold for curved spaces.]]
One of the defining characteristics of a curved space is its departure from the [[Pythagorean theorem]].{{Citation needed|date=January 2024}} In a curved space 
:<math>dx^2 + dy^2 \neq dl^2</math>.

The Pythagorean relationship can often be restored by describing the space with an extra dimension. Suppose we have a three-dimensional [[non-Euclidean space]] with coordinates <math>\left(x',y',z'\right)</math>. Because it is not flat 
:<math>dx'^2 + dy'^2 + dz'^2 \ne dl'^2 \,</math>.

But if we now describe the three-dimensional space with ''four'' dimensions (<math>x,y,z,w</math>) we can ''choose'' coordinates such that 
:<math>dx^2 + dy^2 + dz^2 + dw^2 = dl^2 \,</math>.

Note that the coordinate <math>x</math> is '''not''' the same as the coordinate <math>x'</math>.

For the choice of the 4D coordinates to be valid descriptors of the original 3D space it must have the same number of [[Degrees of freedom (physics and chemistry)|degrees of freedom]]. Since four coordinates have four degrees of freedom it must have a constraint placed on it. We can choose a constraint such that Pythagorean theorem holds in the new 4D space. That is 
:<math>x^2 + y^2 + z^2 +w^2 = \textrm{constant} \,</math>.

The constant can be positive or negative. For convenience we can choose the constant to be 
:<math>\kappa^{-1}R^2</math> where <math>R^2 \,</math> now is positive and <math>\kappa \equiv \plusmn 1</math>.

We can now use this constraint to eliminate the artificial fourth coordinate <math>w</math>. The differential of the constraining equation is 
:<math>xdx + ydy + zdz + wdw = 0 \,</math> leading to <math>dw = -w^{-1}(xdx + ydy +zdz) \,</math>.

Plugging <math>dw</math> into the original equation gives
:<math>dl^2 = dx^2 + dy^2 + dz^2 + \frac{(xdx+ydy+zdz)^2}{\kappa^{-1}R^2 - x^2 - y^2 - z^2}</math>.

This form is usually not particularly appealing and so a coordinate transform is often applied: <math>x = r\sin\theta\cos\phi</math>, <math>y = r\sin\theta\sin\phi</math>, <math>z = r\cos\theta</math>. With this coordinate transformation
:<math>dl^2 = \frac{dr^2}{1-\kappa\frac{r^2}{R^2}} + r^2d\theta^2 + r^2\sin^2\theta d\phi^2</math>.

==Without embedding==
The geometry of a n-dimensional space can also be described with [[Riemannian geometry]]. An [[wiktionary:isotropic|isotropic]] and [[wiktionary:homogeneous|homogeneous]] space can be described by the metric:
:<math>dl^2 = e^{-\lambda(r)}{dr^2} + r^2d\theta^2 + r^2\sin^2\theta d\phi^2 \,</math>.
This reduces to [[Euclidean space]] when <math>\lambda = 0</math>. But a space can be said to be "[[Conformally flat|flat]]" when the [[Weyl tensor]] has all zero components. In three dimensions this condition is met when the [[Ricci curvature|Ricci tensor]] (<math>R_{ab}</math>) is equal to the metric times the [[Scalar curvature|Ricci scalar]] (<math>R</math>, not to be confused with the R of the previous section). That is <math>R_{ab} = g_{ab} R</math>. Calculation of these components from the metric gives that 
:<math>\lambda = -\frac{1}{2}\ln \left( 1 - k r^2 \right)</math> where <math>k \equiv \frac{R}{2}</math>.

This gives the metric:
:<math>dl^2 = \frac{dr^2}{1-k{r^2}} + r^2d\theta^2 + r^2\sin^2\theta d\phi^2</math>.

where <math>k</math> can be zero, positive, or negative and is not limited to ±1.

==Open, flat, closed==
An [[wiktionary:isotropic|isotropic]] and [[wiktionary:homogeneous|homogeneous]] space can be described by the metric:{{Citation needed|date=January 2024}}
:<math>dl^2 = \frac{dr^2}{1-\kappa\frac{r^2}{R^2}} + r^2d\theta^2 + r^2\sin^2\theta d\phi^2</math>.

In the limit that the constant of curvature (<math>R</math>) becomes infinitely large, a flat, [[Euclidean space]] is returned. It is essentially the same as setting <math>\kappa</math> to zero. If <math>\kappa</math> is not zero the space is not Euclidean. When <math>\kappa = +1</math> the space is said to be ''closed'' or [[Elliptic geometry|elliptic]]. When <math>\kappa = -1</math> the space is said to be ''open'' or [[Hyperbolic geometry|hyperbolic]].

Triangles which lie on the surface of an open space will have a sum of angles which is less than 180°. Triangles which lie on the surface of a closed space will have a sum of angles which is greater than 180°. The volume, however, is '''not''' <math>(4/3)\pi r^3</math>.
